p: Big-O describes how the cost grows as the input grows, discarding constants and lower-order terms. An O(n) algorithm that does a hundred operations per element is slower than an O(n squared) algorithm for every input below a certain size, and that size is frequently small enough to matter. The notation is a tool for comparing growth rates, not a ranking of implementations. The practical question is always: for the sizes I actually see, which approach wins, and where is the crossover point?

The common growth rates in order are constant, logarithmic, linear, linearithmic, quadratic, exponential and factorial. Logarithmic algorithms halve the problem each step, so binary search over a million items takes about twenty comparisons. Linearithmic is the cost of a comparison sort. Quadratic appears whenever a loop contains a loop over the same data, and it is the single most common performance defect in application code: an inner lookup that scans an array, a filter inside a map, a nested find over a nested collection. Most quadratic code in real applications is accidental and disappears when a Set or a Map replaces a scan.

Amortised cost is a separate concept from worst-case cost and both matter. Array push is O(1) amortised because occasional resizes are paid for across many cheap operations, but any single push can be O(n) when the backing store grows. A hash map lookup is O(1) on average and O(n) in the worst case when every key collides. Quoting the average without the worst case is how a system passes load tests and then falls over on adversarial input, so for anything exposed to untrusted keys, treat the worst case as the one to design against.

Space complexity is measured the same way and is often the real constraint. An algorithm that is O(n) in time and O(n) in extra space may be unusable on a device with a small heap, while an in-place version that is O(n log n) in time and O(log n) in space fits. Recursion adds stack space proportional to depth, so a recursive traversal of a deeply nested structure can exhaust the stack where an explicit stack with a heap-allocated array would not. State both dimensions when you choose, and note that strings and objects in JavaScript carry more per-element overhead than a typed array does.

Input size is not always the obvious dimension. For a string algorithm the relevant size may be the number of bytes, the number of code points or the number of grapheme clusters, and the three differ. For a graph the size is usually the number of vertices plus the number of edges, often written as O(V + E), and an algorithm that is linear in V but quadratic in E behaves very differently on a dense graph than on a sparse one. Naming the dimension explicitly is half of getting the analysis right.

Finally, complexity analysis assumes an operation model that the language does not always honour. In JavaScript, array element access is constant time only for a packed array of the same kind of value; a sparse array or a mixed array of objects and numbers can degrade to a dictionary-like store. Property access on an object shaped inconsistently across call sites defeats the engine's inline caches and can cost several times more. The algorithm is the first-order effect and the representation is the second-order one, and both are needed to predict real performance.

Wall-clock timing of a whole function is a poor instrument because it mixes setup, garbage collection and the rest of the machine. performance.now returns a high-resolution timestamp suitable for durations, and the difference of two reads is the standard measurement. Repeat the work many times and report a percentile rather than a single sample, because the first run is dominated by JIT compilation and warm-up and the maximum is usually an unrelated interrupt. Discard a warm-up phase, take several hundred iterations, and report the median or the ninth decile.

Microbenchmarks mislead more often than they inform. The JIT compiler optimises based on the observed types in a way that differs from production, dead code can be eliminated so a benchmark measures nothing, and an inlined loop in a hot function behaves differently from the same loop spread across modules. When a microbenchmark says a construct is faster, treat the result as a hypothesis to confirm with a profile of the real application rather than a conclusion. If the difference is under a few tens of percent, it will be swamped by everything else.

Profiling answers the question a benchmark cannot: where did the time actually go. A sampling profiler records the call stack at a fixed interval and aggregates the samples into a tree, so the leaf frames with the most self time are the ones doing the work. A flame graph renders that tree with width proportional to time and depth proportional to stack depth; a wide frame near the top means many calls, a wide frame near the bottom means an expensive leaf. Read the graph from the widest frames inward, not from the code you happen to suspect.

Counters are the other half of the picture. Number of allocations, garbage collections per second, bytes allocated per request and event loop delay together explain a performance problem that a profile shows but does not diagnose. A function that is hot and allocates heavily is a candidate for reuse; a function that is hot and does not allocate is a candidate for an algorithmic change. Node's perf_hooks module exposes both the histogram for delay and the performance observer for measuring named marks and measures.

Beware the measurement changing the thing measured. A console.log in a hot path dominates the cost of the path. Adding a counter to a loop that runs millions of times per second can double its time. Measuring the memory of a large object by serialising it is itself an allocation. Guard the instrumentation behind a flag, keep the counters numeric and cheap, and prefer sampling to instrumenting when the code path is very hot. If the measurement is only enabled in development, it can be richer.

Finally, decide the acceptance threshold before you optimise. A page that renders in two hundred milliseconds is not improved in any way a user can perceive by making it one hundred and eighty. Optimise against a stated budget and a stated percentile, for example a ninety-fifth percentile response under two hundred milliseconds, and stop when the budget is met. Without a budget, optimisation becomes an unbounded activity that trades clarity for a difference nobody can feel and that the next dependency update can erase.

The choice of data structure usually dominates the choice of algorithm. Membership testing is the clearest case: Array.prototype.includes is a linear scan, so a filter over a list that checks membership in another array is quadratic, while a Set turns the same work linear. The same transformation applies to counting with an object or Map instead of filtering for each key, to grouping with a Map instead of repeated finds, and to looking up a record by id in a Map instead of in an array. These four rewrites remove the majority of accidental quadratic behaviour in application code.

Arrays win when order matters, when you need random access by position, when the data is small, or when you iterate the whole collection far more often than you look things up. Elements are stored contiguously, iteration is fast and predictable, and the engine optimises array access heavily. Insertion and removal in the middle are linear because the tail has to move, so a queue built on Array.prototype.shift is quadratic over the whole sequence even though each call looks cheap. Use a dedicated deque or an index-pointer technique for that pattern.

Maps and Sets are the general-purpose lookup structures. Map preserves insertion order, allows any key including objects and NaN, and exposes size directly. Plain objects are faster to create and are the right representation for records with a known shape and string keys, but they require Object.keys to count, coerce keys to strings, and inherit prototype properties unless created with Object.create(null) or a null-prototype literal. Use a Map whenever the key is not a string, whenever the insertion order is meaningful, or whenever the collection is genuinely a collection rather than a record.

Typed arrays are the right tool for numeric data at scale. A Float64Array of a million values uses eight megabytes of contiguous memory and has no per-element boxing, while a plain array of the same numbers is substantially larger and slower to sum. Typed arrays have a fixed length, so they cannot grow, and they do not sort with the comparison semantics of a normal array. For graphics, signal processing, binary protocols and numeric kernels, they are the correct choice; for ordinary business data they are unnecessary complexity.

Specialised structures earn their place when a specific operation dominates. A heap gives constant-time access to the minimum and logarithmic insertion, which a sorted array cannot match because every insertion is linear. A trie gives prefix queries in time proportional to the prefix length, which a hash map cannot express at all. A doubly linked list gives constant-time removal of a known node, which arrays cannot. Reach for one when the profile shows the operation is hot; before that, the simpler structure with the better constant factor usually wins.

The decisive test is usually not time complexity but the shape of the access pattern. Write down the operations the code performs, how often each one runs, and the size of the collection, then pick the structure whose cheap operations are the frequent ones. This is a five-minute exercise that replaces hours of profiling, and the answer is frequently that the collection is small enough that any structure works and readability should decide. Optimising a hundred-element list with a trie is a cost with no benefit.

A stack is last in, first out, and in JavaScript an array is already a perfectly good stack: push adds to the end, pop removes from the end, and both are constant-time amortised. Nothing else is needed. The reasons to write a Stack class are to make the intent explicit in a domain that is genuinely a stack, and to hide the array so that no caller can reach into the middle. A stack that answers only push, pop, peek and isEmpty documents the intended use and prevents a maintainer from indexing into it.

Stacks appear wherever the most recent unfinished thing is the next thing to do: matching brackets, evaluating a postfix expression, converting infix to postfix with the shunting-yard algorithm, undo histories, depth-first traversal, and the call stack itself. The bracket-matching case is the canonical one: push every opening delimiter, and on a closing delimiter check that the top of the stack is its partner and pop, ending with an empty stack. The version that counts openers instead of pushing characters fails on interleaved types such as a closing bracket that matches an earlier opener.

The most valuable use of a stack in application code is turning recursion into iteration. An explicit stack avoids the call stack limit, which matters for a deeply nested tree or an unbounded directory walk. The transformation is mechanical: replace the recursive call with a push, and the return path with a pop. Order matters — pushing children in reverse gives the same visit order as the recursive version, which is the detail that trips people up when the output silently comes out mirrored.

A monotonic stack keeps its contents in sorted order and answers next-greater or next-smaller element queries in linear time. For each element, pop while the top violates the ordering, then the top is the answer for the current element, then push. This solves the daily-temperatures problem, the largest-rectangle-in-a-histogram problem and span calculations, all of which look quadratic at first glance. Recognising the shape is what matters: a query about the nearest element that satisfies a comparison is usually a monotonic stack.

A stack is also the natural model for a parser. A recursive-descent parser uses the call stack; a table-driven parser uses an explicit stack of states and symbols. In text processing, a stack handles nested structures such as markup tags, code fences and parenthesised expressions, where the requirement is to know the current nesting context and to detect an unbalanced close. Reaching for a counter instead of a stack is only valid when there is a single delimiter type, which is rarely the case in real input.

The failure mode to guard against is unbounded growth. A stack that only ever receives pushes and never pops is a memory leak shaped like a data structure. Any loop that pushes without a matching pop must have a bound, and any parser must decide what to do on an unbalanced close: recover by ignoring, recover by closing the outer context, or reject. Choosing explicitly at design time is much cheaper than discovering the behaviour by feeding the parser a truncated file in production.

A queue is first in, first out, and a plain array is a poor queue. push and shift together are quadratic over the whole sequence because shift moves every remaining element down one index. For a handful of items it is fine; for a queue of a hundred thousand tasks it is the dominant cost. The two standard fixes are a deque backed by an object with head and tail indices, and a fixed-size ring buffer. Both give constant-time enqueue and dequeue and both are about twenty lines of code.

An index-pointer queue keeps the backing array and an integer head. Enqueue is push and dequeue is a read at head followed by an increment. The array still grows and never shrinks, so it is appropriate for a bounded burst and not for a queue that runs forever. Adding a compaction step that copies the live suffix back to the front when head exceeds some threshold keeps memory proportional to the live size, at the cost of an occasional linear copy that is still amortised constant.

A ring buffer preallocates a fixed capacity, keeps head, tail and size, and wraps the indices modulo the capacity. It is the right structure for a bounded queue, a sliding window of recent events, or a log buffer, and it makes the memory bound explicit and testable. Enqueue on a full ring either drops the oldest element or rejects, and that decision is a policy the caller should make rather than a detail hidden in the implementation. A ring buffer is also the fastest way to keep the last n measurements for a percentile calculation.

A deque supports push and pop at both ends in constant time, which makes it both a queue and a stack. The classic use is the sliding-window maximum: maintain a deque of indices whose values are decreasing, pop from the back while the new value is larger, pop from the front while the front is outside the window, and the front is the maximum. This is linear where the naive version is quadratic, and it generalises to any windowed aggregate whose combining operation is associative and idempotent enough to allow removal.

Priority queues are a different structure, covered with heaps, and the temptation to fake one by sorting is worth naming. Sorting the whole collection on every insert is linearithmic per insert; inserting into a sorted array with binary search plus a splice is linear per insert because of the shift; a binary heap is logarithmic per insert and constant to peek. Task schedulers, rate limiters that must consider deadlines, and any algorithm described as taking the cheapest first should use a heap rather than an array that is re-sorted.

Whatever structure you choose, name the operations after the domain. A queue of retry attempts reads better with enqueue and dequeue than with push and shift, and the wrapper is the place to add the bound, the metric and the policy for a full buffer. The structure itself is a dozen lines; the value is in the intent and the invariants it makes checkable, and in the fact that swapping the implementation later does not require touching the callers.

A singly linked list stores a value and a reference to the next node, with the head kept by the caller. It gives constant-time insertion and removal at a known node, which arrays cannot, and it wastes memory on the pointer and loses locality of reference, which arrays do not. In a language with a garbage collector and no pointer arithmetic, the honest uses are a queue with an explicit tail pointer, an LRU cache with a doubly linked list plus a hash map, and a free list that reuses nodes.

Traversal is the same loop in every operation: keep a previous pointer, a current pointer and sometimes a next pointer, and update them in the right order. Reversing a list is the canonical exercise and it is worth knowing by heart, because the same three-pointer dance appears in removal and in-place partitioning. The detail that breaks implementations is saving the next reference before overwriting the current node's next pointer, since overwriting first loses the rest of the list and produces a single-element list that looks correct until you print it.

A doubly linked list adds a previous pointer so removal is constant-time given the node, and so iteration can go backwards. The LRU cache is its showcase application: a hash map from key to node gives constant lookup, the list orders nodes by recency, a hit moves the node to the front, and an insert that exceeds the capacity evicts the tail. Every operation is constant time, which is exactly what the doubly linked list buys over an array where moving a node to the front would be linear.

Sentinel nodes remove the special cases that make list code fragile. A permanent head node and a permanent tail node mean every insertion and removal happens between two real nodes, so there is no branch for the empty list and none for the first or last element. The code becomes uniform and the bugs disappear. The cost is one extra node and a slightly denser mental model, and it is a trade worth making whenever the list is a core data structure rather than a curiosity.

Cycle detection is a required safety check. A list that accidentally points backwards turns any traversal into an infinite loop that eventually exhausts memory. Floyd's tortoise-and-hare detects a cycle in linear time with constant space by advancing one pointer by one and another by two and checking whether they meet. The same technique finds the start of a cycle and the length of the repeated segment. In applications, the practical version is usually a visited Set or a depth limit, but knowing the constant-space method matters when the data is large.

Finally, remember that what you actually want is often not a linked list. When the reason for considering one is fast removal from the middle, ask whether an order-statistics tree or a skip list would be more appropriate; when it is ordered iteration with cheap insertion, an array plus periodic sorting may be simpler; when it is a queue, a deque or ring buffer beats a list on memory and locality. A linked list earns its place when the node identity is stable across removals and the order is maintained by relinking, and that is a narrower requirement than it first appears.

A hash table maps a key to a bucket index by computing a hash and reducing it modulo the bucket count. Collisions are inevitable because the space of keys is larger than the space of buckets, so the table must store multiple entries per bucket, usually as a linked chain or as open addressing with probing. The average case is constant time when the keys are spread evenly and the load factor — the ratio of entries to buckets — is kept low. When the load factor exceeds a threshold the table grows and rehashes every key.

JavaScript gives you no direct access to the hash table, but understanding it explains the behaviour of Map, Set and objects. Insertion order is preserved in Map and Set because the specification requires it, which means they are ordered hash tables internally rather than pure ones. Object property order follows a rule: integer-like keys in ascending numeric order first, then string keys in insertion order, then symbols. That rule is why an object with numeric-looking keys does not iterate in the order you inserted them and why a Map is the right choice when order is meaningful.

The load factor is why a hash table lookup can be slower than an array index even though both are constant time. Resizing is amortised but has a visible spike, which is why latency-sensitive code preallocates or warms up. A table sized to a power of two allows the modulo to be a bitwise AND and is what most library implementations use, with the mixing step doing the work of spreading the high bits before masking. A poor mixing function concentrates keys and turns the average case into the worst case.

Hash quality matters most for keys an attacker controls. Strings hash by a deterministic algorithm, so an adversary who can choose the keys can, in principle, force many of them into the same bucket and degrade every lookup to a linear scan. Mitigations are a randomised seed per process and a strong mixing function; modern engines use both, and the string hash in V8 is computed lazily and cached on the string object. When you build a hash table yourself for untrusted keys, include a random per-process seed.

For custom objects, structural sharing and interning reduce cost. A value that is recreated with the same content hashes to the same number if the hash is content-based, but two objects that are not identical have different identity, so a plain object or Map keyed by object reference treats them as distinct. Content-based keying requires you to derive a stable string or number key yourself and to accept the collision risk of the extracted fields. This is a design decision with correctness consequences, not a micro-optimisation.

The practical takeaways are short. Choose a Map over an object when keys are not strings or order matters. Choose a Set over an array for membership. Keep string keys short if you build millions of them, because hashing is proportional to length. Avoid using large composite strings as keys when a small tuple would do, since the hash walks the whole string. And remember that a nested object as a key means reference identity, which is almost never what the author intended.

s.t: Map, Set and WeakMap in depth
p: Map has get, set, has, delete, clear, size and an ordered iterator over entries, keys or values. It accepts any value as a key, including NaN, which it matches to itself unlike the SameValueZero comparison used elsewhere; -0 and +0 are the same key. Keys are compared by identity for objects, so two structurally identical objects are two different keys. Map is a proper iterable, so it spreads, destructures and works with for-of directly, and constructing from an array of pairs gives you a conversion from a plain record.

Set stores unique values with the same key comparison rules and exposes add, has, delete, clear, size and ordered iteration. The useful patterns are deduplication, membership, and set algebra that you write yourself because the standard library does not provide union, intersection or difference. Building those as small functions over Sets is straightforward: union by spreading into a new Set, intersection by filtering one Set against has on the other, difference by filtering with the negation. They are linear rather than the quadratic version that filters arrays against arrays.

WeakMap and WeakSet hold keys weakly, so an entry disappears once the key is otherwise unreachable and the garbage collector runs. This is the mechanism for attaching metadata to an object without preventing its collection, which is exactly what the classic pattern of adding a hidden property does and why that pattern leaks. Both are non-iterable and have no size, because the contents can change at any moment as the collector runs; a size that changes asynchronously is not something you can reason about, so the API deliberately omits it.

The standard use for a WeakMap is private state. A module-level WeakMap from an instance to a record of its private fields gives genuine encapsulation without a property that reflection can find, and the entry is released with the instance. It is also how a library memoises per-object: a WeakMap from the object to its computed result, so the result lives exactly as long as the object does. A regular Map for the same purpose is a leak, because the key is retained forever and the map grows with every distinct object ever seen.

The Map versus object decision has a performance edge worth knowing. An object with a fixed shape is faster to read and write than a Map because the engine can use an inline cache keyed on the property's position; a Map has a method call and a lookup. Conversely, a Map with many keys, non-string keys, frequent additions and deletions, or a need for ordering is faster and clearer than an object whose shape is constantly changing, since every new key on an object invalidates the shape and can force the engine to rebuild the hidden class.

Converting between the two is a common boundary operation. Object.fromEntries(map) turns a Map of string keys into a plain object, and new Map(Object.entries(obj)) does the reverse. Note that Object.fromEntries only keeps string and symbol keys, so a Map with object keys loses information silently when converted. A convenient helper is a Next-style custom type with a nullable internal map, because representing an absent value with null rather than undefined catches the case where the caller forgot to check, and TypeScript then forces the check.

When an object must be a key by content rather than by identity, derive a canonical string. The recipe is to pick the identifying fields, sort them, encode each as name and value with a separator that cannot appear in the values, and join. Using JSON.stringify of a sorted field list is the common shortcut and it is acceptable for simple values, but it is order-sensitive unless you sort the keys, it cannot distinguish a missing field from an undefined one in some encodings, and its output can be ambiguous for values that contain the separators.

A better approach is an explicit encode function that escapes the delimiters. For fields joined by the unit separator character, replace occurrences of that character and of the escape character in each value first, then join. This is the same principle as CSV quoting. The function should be pure and documented, because its output is now an implicit cache key or database key and a change to it invalidates every stored key. Versioning the encoding, perhaps by prefixing a schema version, makes that migration explicit instead of silent.

Numeric composite keys are a faster option when the components are bounded. Pack the fields into a single number with bit shifts and masks, which is exact while the total width stays within the safe integer range, and falls back to BigInt beyond it. Packing gives a key that compares and sorts numerically and hashes cheaply, and it is the standard technique for grid coordinates, tile identifiers and spatial buckets. The cost in readability is real, so keep the pack and unpack functions adjacent and unit-tested.

A two-level Map is sometimes cleaner than an encoded key. A Map from the first component to an inner Map from the second avoids the encoding problem entirely, keeps the components typed, and allows iterating one dimension efficiently. The trade is more allocation and a more awkward delete, which must prune the inner map when it becomes empty. When the components are naturally nested and both are frequently accessed alone, the nested form is the better shape; when the key is read as a whole, the encoded form is.

Hash collisions for derived keys are a correctness question only for fixed-size hashes. If you hash a composite to a 32-bit integer for speed, collisions are possible and must be handled by storing the original key alongside and comparing on retrieval. The two-level pattern of hash then verify is what every hash table does internally, and it is what you must do if you choose a lossy key. A key that is guaranteed lossless needs no verification, which is why the canonical-string approach is the safer default.

Finally, decide the lifetime of any cache keyed by derived values. A Map that grows forever with derived keys is a memory leak that is much harder to spot than one with a single long-lived key, because each entry looks small and reasonable. Add an explicit size bound with an eviction policy, use a WeakMap when the key is an object you already retain elsewhere, and instrument the size. Every unbounded cache is a slow-motion outage, and the only question is how long the growth takes.

A binary search tree keeps the invariant that every value in the left subtree is smaller than the node and every value in the right subtree is larger. Lookup, insert and delete are then proportional to the height of the tree: logarithmic when balanced and linear when it degenerates into a path, which is what a sequence of sorted insertions produces. That degeneration is the entire reason balanced variants such as the red-black tree and the AVL tree exist, and it is why an unbalanced search tree should not be used with ordered input.

Traversal has three depth-first orders with distinct uses. In-order visits the left subtree, the node, then the right, and produces the values in sorted order, which is the single most useful property of the structure. Pre-order visits the node first, which is what you need to serialise a tree so it can be rebuilt. Post-order visits the node last, which is what you need when a computation at a node depends on the results from its children — directory sizes, expression evaluation and dependency resolution all use it.

Breadth-first traversal uses a queue rather than a stack and visits the tree level by level. It is the basis of the shortest path in an unweighted graph, of level-order printing and of any algorithm that wants the nearest node first. The implementation difference from depth-first is a single line: pushing the children onto a queue instead of a stack. Keeping the level boundary explicit, by recording the queue length at the start of each level, is what lets you compute per-level aggregates without extra bookkeeping.

Deletion has three cases and the third is where implementations usually break. A leaf is removed directly. A node with one child is replaced by that child. A node with two children is replaced by either its in-order successor — the smallest value in the right subtree — or its in-order predecessor, and then the successor's original position is removed, recursively, which is the one-child or leaf case. Copying the successor's value and deleting the successor is simpler than relinking and is adequate when node identity does not matter, which is most of the time.

Balanced trees are usually unnecessary in application code because a sorted array and binary search cover the read-mostly case and a Map covers the keyed access case. The balanced tree earns its place when you need ordered iteration and logarithmic insertion and deletion together, when you need range queries such as all keys between two bounds, or when you need order statistics such as the k-th smallest. That combination is exactly what a database index provides, which is why the pragmatic answer in a web application is often to let the database do it.

When you do implement one, keep the balancing logic isolated and test the invariant directly. A balanced tree is correct when every node's subtree heights differ by at most a small bound and the search property holds, and both are cheap to check with a recursive validator. Property-based testing with random insertion and deletion sequences finds rotation bugs far more reliably than hand-written cases. The validator itself must be simple enough to trust, because a validator that shares the bug proves nothing.

A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array, where every parent is smaller than or equal to its children in a min-heap. Because it is complete, the array representation is exact and no pointers are needed: for the element at index i, its children are at two i plus one and two i plus two, and its parent is at the floor of i minus one divided by two. Peek is constant time, and insert and remove-min are logarithmic because a single path from the leaf or root is walked while swapping.

Sift-up and sift-down are the only two operations. Insert appends at the end and sifts up while the parent is larger, swapping each time. Remove-min replaces the root with the last element, shrinks the array and sifts down while a child is smaller, swapping with the smaller child so the invariant is restored along one path only. The choice of the smaller child is what makes sift-down correct; swapping with the larger one produces a structure that is not a heap and that fails only for particular shapes.

Building a heap from an existing array is linear, not linearithmic, if you sift down from the last non-leaf back to the root rather than inserting one element at a time. This is the basis of heapsort, which is in-place and O(n log n) in the worst case but has poor cache behaviour compared with quicksort and is not stable. In practice heapsort's real value is as the safety net in a hybrid sort that switches to it when quicksort's recursion depth grows too large, which is how most library sorts avoid the quadratic worst case.

A priority queue is a heap with the operations named for the domain: enqueue with a priority, dequeue the highest priority, peek the highest priority. The comparator decides what highest means, and passing the comparator in rather than baking in an ordering is what makes the structure reusable. A stable priority queue also records insertion order and breaks ties by that, which matters when equal priorities should be processed in arrival order — a scheduler that does not do this reorders equal-priority jobs arbitrarily.

The classic applications are scheduling and streaming. Dijkstra's and A* search both maintain a frontier ordered by tentative cost. A k-way merge of sorted inputs uses a heap of the current head of each input. A streaming median uses two heaps, a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper, rebalanced after every insertion so their sizes differ by at most one; the median is then the top of one or the average of both tops. Top-k is a heap of size k with the smallest of the retained elements at the root.

Implementing it in JavaScript means writing the comparator carefully. A comparator that returns a boolean instead of a number is the most common defect: the sift loop tests a relational expression, which coerces, and the result is a heap that is subtly wrong for some inputs and correct for others. Return the difference or the result of the comparison operators, and unit-test with a random shuffle followed by repeated remove-min to verify the output is sorted. That test catches essentially every insertion, removal and comparator bug in one stroke.

A trie stores strings character by character along edges, with a node per prefix. Lookup, insert and delete run in time proportional to the length of the string, independent of how many strings are stored, which is what distinguishes it from a hash table where a longer key costs more to hash and where prefix queries are impossible. The price is memory: one node per distinct prefix, which for many short strings with few shared prefixes can be far more than the strings themselves.

Each node either stores a map from the next character to the child and a flag marking the end of a word, or uses a fixed 26-slot array for lowercase ASCII. The map version uses less memory for sparse alphabets and supports arbitrary Unicode; the array version is faster and is appropriate when the alphabet is known to be small. Marking the end of a word is essential and is separate from having children, because a word can be a prefix of another and both are stored in the same path.

Prefix search is the operation a trie exists for. Walk the prefix, then collect all words below that node with a depth-first traversal. Autocomplete, spell-check candidate generation, IP routing tables with longest-prefix match, and dictionary word games all reduce to this. The collect step should take a limit so a query for the empty prefix does not traverse the entire dictionary, and should terminate early once the limit is reached rather than building the full list and slicing it.

A compressed trie, or radix tree, collapses chains of single-child nodes into a single edge labelled with a substring. This reduces the node count dramatically for a typical word list and is what a production routing table or a JSON router often uses. The implementation is more delicate because edges must be split when a new key diverges in the middle of an existing label, but the trade is worth it whenever memory matters. A ternary search tree is the alternative that keeps three children per node and stores one character per node, giving a smaller footprint with slightly slower lookups.

A suffix trie indexes every suffix of a text so that any substring query becomes a prefix walk. Building it naively costs quadratic time and memory, which is why the suffix array and the Burrows-Wheeler transform are the practical structures for full-text indexing at scale. This is the layer beneath a search engine: the inverted index maps tokens to document lists, and the FTS index in a database is exactly that, which is why a keyword search using an index is logarithmic and a substring scan is linear.

The practical lesson is to reach for a trie when prefix queries are part of the requirement and for a hash structure otherwise. Most applications need autocomplete once, and a sorted array of strings with a binary search for the prefix range gives prefix queries with far less code and often better cache behaviour. A trie wins when the collection changes frequently, when the strings are long and share prefixes, or when memory for the index is not the constraint. Choose it for those reasons, not because it is interesting.

A graph is a set of vertices and a set of edges, and the two standard representations trade memory for lookup speed. An adjacency list stores, for each vertex, a collection of its neighbours, which uses memory proportional to the number of edges and is the right choice for sparse graphs. An adjacency matrix stores a boolean or weight per pair, which uses memory proportional to the square of the vertex count and gives constant-time edge lookup. Most real graphs are sparse, so the adjacency list is the default.

In JavaScript the adjacency list is a Map from a vertex identifier to an array or Set of neighbours. A Map keyed by the vertex value handles non-numeric and non-contiguous identifiers without the wasted array slots that indexing by number would create. A Set of neighbours makes duplicate-edge insertion idempotent and edge lookup linear in the degree; an array is smaller and faster to iterate but allows duplicates. For weighted graphs the neighbour value becomes an object or a tuple of target and weight, and iterating it is the inner loop of every algorithm.

Directedness and weights must be explicit in the model rather than implied by the data. One-way edges appear in dependency graphs, in hyperlink graphs and in state machines. Undirected edges are stored twice, once in each direction, and the code that does so must be in a single function so the symmetry cannot be broken. Negative weights change which algorithm is valid, since Dijkstra assumes non-negative weight; a negative edge requires Bellman-Ford, which is slower but tolerant of them and can also detect a negative cycle.

Reading a graph from a table of edges is the usual integration point. Each row names a source and a target and possibly a weight, and the build function should validate that identifiers are present and that no edge references an undeclared vertex. Storing the vertex list explicitly rather than deriving it from the edges matters for isolated vertices, which have no edges and would otherwise vanish. Degree counts, connected components and topological order all need the full vertex set, not just the ones that happen to appear in an edge.

For grid-shaped problems the graph is implicit and does not need to be built. A two-dimensional grid of cells is a graph whose neighbours are the up, down, left and right cells in bounds, and the traversal carries the coordinates rather than a node object. This is the representation to prefer whenever the graph is regular, because storing an adjacency list for a grid wastes memory on a structure that can be computed. The same applies to an ordered sequence of states, where the edges are simply the next index.

Representing a graph also invites the reverse question: do you need one at all? A tree is a graph, but a tree has a unique parent and can be stored as a plain nested object or a flat list with parent pointers, which is far simpler than a general adjacency structure. Reaching for the general tool when the data is a tree, a list or a grid is a common source of unnecessary complexity, and the simplest representation that supports the required operations is the right one.

Breadth-first search visits a graph in order of distance from the source when every edge has the same weight. It uses a queue, marks a vertex when it is enqueued rather than when it is dequeued, and therefore finds the shortest number of edges to every reachable vertex. Marking on dequeue instead of enqueue is the classic bug: it lets a vertex be enqueued several times, which turns a linear traversal into something much worse and can duplicate work exponentially on a dense graph.

Depth-first search uses a stack, either explicitly or through recursion, and is the right tool for connectivity, cycle detection, topological ordering and strongly connected components. A colour marking with white, grey and black states distinguishes an unexplored vertex from one on the current path from one fully explored; an edge to a grey vertex is a back edge and therefore a cycle. In an undirected graph a back edge means a cycle, and in a directed graph it means a cycle too, which is the basis of cycle detection in a dependency graph.

Topological sort orders a directed acyclic graph so that every edge points forward. Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes a vertex with no incoming edges, which also detects a cycle because a non-empty graph with no such vertex contains one. The depth-first variant emits vertices in reverse post-order. Build systems, task schedulers, migration orderings and package installation all use this, and the required companion output is which vertices were left over when a cycle was detected, because that set is the deadlock to break.

Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths with non-negative weights by repeatedly extracting the nearest unsettled vertex from a priority queue and relaxing its outgoing edges. With a binary heap it is linearithmic in the edge count, which is good enough for almost every application. Without a priority queue it degrades to quadratic, which is fine only for tiny graphs. The relaxation step must compare the newly computed distance with the stored one and update only when it is smaller, and the stored distance for an unreached vertex should be Infinity so the comparison works without a special case.

A* adds a heuristic that estimates the remaining cost to the goal and orders the frontier by the sum of the known cost and the estimate. With an admissible heuristic that never overestimates, A* finds the optimal path while exploring fewer vertices than Dijkstra. On a grid, Manhattan or Euclidean distance is the natural heuristic; for a road network, straight-line distance divided by the maximum speed is. A heuristic that overestimates makes the search faster and the answer wrong, which is a trade that should be made deliberately rather than accidentally.

When edges have negative weights, use Bellman-Ford: relax every edge repeatedly for as many rounds as there are vertices, and if a further relaxation is still possible the graph contains a negative cycle reachable from the source. For all-pairs shortest paths on a small dense graph, Floyd-Warshall runs three nested loops over the vertex count and is the simplest correct implementation. Above a few hundred vertices it becomes impractical, and the right answer is usually to run Dijkstra from each vertex or to change the problem.

Array.prototype.sort sorts in place and converts every element to a string by default, which is why [10, 9, 80].sort() produces [10, 80, 9]. A comparator must be supplied for anything that is not a string, and the comparator must return a negative number, zero or a positive number. The specification now requires a stable sort, so equal elements keep their relative order and a multi-key sort can be composed by sorting by the least significant key first. The engine uses a hybrid that switches strategies on the size and shape of the input.

The taught comparison sorts are quicksort, mergesort and heapsort. Quicksort partitions around a pivot and is the fastest in practice because of cache behaviour, but it is quadratic on adversarial input unless the pivot is chosen randomly or by median-of-three. Mergesort is stable and predictable at O(n log n) but needs auxiliary space. Heapsort is in place and worst-case optimal but has poor locality. The non-comparison sorts — counting sort, radix sort and bucket sort — can beat all three when the key space is small and bounded, which is common for integers.

Writing a correct quicksort means getting the partition right, and there are two schemes worth knowing. Lomuto's partition is four lines and does more swaps; Hoare's is subtler and does fewer. Both must guarantee termination when many elements are equal to the pivot, which is why the modern advice is a three-way partition into less than, equal and greater than. Without it, an array of identical values produces the worst case on the standard two-way scheme. This is the single most common quicksort bug.

Binary search finds a value in a sorted array in logarithmic time, and the implementation that is correct is worth memorising: low and high indices, a loop while low is less than or equal to high, a midpoint from the floor of the average, and three branches that either return, set high to mid minus one, or set low to mid plus one. The midpoint must be computed as low plus the floor of the difference divided by two rather than as the average of low and high, because the sum can exceed the safe integer range on huge arrays. Off-by-one bugs in the bounds are the other classic failure.

Binary search also answers questions that are not equality tests. Leftmost and rightmost insertion points, the smallest value satisfying a predicate, and lower and upper bounds over a monotonic function all reduce to the same loop with a different comparison. A binary search over the answer space solves optimisation problems whose feasibility check is monotonic, such as finding the smallest capacity that allows a schedule to complete. Recognising that a predicate is monotonic is what makes that technique available.

Searching an unsorted collection is linear by definition, so the right move is often to build an index rather than search harder. A Set for membership, a Map for keyed lookup, a sorted array plus binary search for repeated range queries, and a database index for anything persisted. Building an index costs one pass and turns every subsequent query from linear to constant or logarithmic. That single decision, made once at load time, is usually a larger win than any improvement to the search itself.

A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input and combines the results. Every call consumes a stack frame, so the depth is bounded by the runtime's stack size, which in JavaScript is on the order of ten thousand frames and varies by engine and by how much each frame holds. Exceeding it throws a RangeError about the maximum call stack size, and the error is not catchable in a useful way because the stack is already exhausted. Deep recursion over a linked list or a deep tree must therefore be converted to iteration with an explicit stack.

Tail calls are not optimised in JavaScript. A call in tail position does not grow the stack in a language with proper tail calls, but the specification's guarantee was effectively removed before shipping and no mainstream engine implements it. Writing a function in tail-recursive style is still good practice for clarity, but it will not save you from the stack limit. Converting to a loop with an explicit accumulator is the portable form and it is what the engine would do anyway if it supported tail calls.

Divide and conquer is the recursion pattern that pays. Split the input into halves, solve each recursively, combine the results. Mergesort, quicksort, binary search, the closest-pair problem and the fast Fourier transform all follow it, and the recurrence for the running time yields linearithmic or better. When the split is uneven, the analysis changes: a recursion that removes a constant number of elements per step is linear, and one that removes a constant fraction is logarithmic, and confusing the two is how a supposedly fast algorithm turns out to be quadratic.

Memoisation turns an exponential recursion into a polynomial one when the same subproblem recurs. Fibonacci is the standard example: the naive version recomputes each value many times and runs in exponential time, while caching the result per input index makes it linear. The cache must be keyed on everything the result depends on, and the function must be pure for the cache to be valid. A function that reads mutable state or the current time cannot be memoised without including that state in the key, otherwise the cache returns stale answers.

The stack depth itself is often the design constraint. A recursive descent over a deeply nested document needs a depth limit that produces a clear error rather than a crash, and the limit should be low enough to leave room for the rest of the call graph. An incremental parser that maintains an explicit stack on the heap can have a depth limit in the tens of thousands, because heap memory is far larger than the stack, and that is the right design for anything that consumes untrusted input of arbitrary shape.

The most practical advice is to write the recursive version first because it is clearer, then convert to iteration only where the depth is genuinely unbounded or the profile shows the allocations matter. A recursive tree walk over a configuration that is four levels deep is fine forever. A recursive walk over a parse tree built from user input is a stack overflow waiting to happen. The distinction is about the input's bound, not about recursion in general, and it should be a conscious decision rather than a style preference.

Memoisation is a cache keyed on the arguments of a pure function, and its validity depends entirely on that purity. The standard wrapper serialises the arguments into a key, checks the cache, computes on a miss and stores. JSON.stringify of the argument array is the common key derivation and it fails on functions, on undefined values that disappear from a serialised array, on values that stringify identically but differ, and on property order. A hand-written key function for the specific arguments is safer whenever the shape is known.

The cache should be a Map rather than an object, so keys can be of any type and insertion order is preserved for eviction. A plain object forces string keys, shares the prototype chain, and has surprising behaviour for keys such as __proto__. A WeakMap is the right choice when the single argument is an object and the memoised result should live exactly as long as that object, which avoids an unbounded cache entirely. For multiple object arguments, nest WeakMaps or fall back to a bounded Map.

The hardest part is bounding the cache. An unbounded memo is a memory leak with a friendly name, and it is a common one because the growth is invisible until it is fatal. Options are a maximum size with least-recently-used eviction, a time-to-live, or a WeakMap where the key lifetime governs. LRU eviction needs the access order, which a Map gives for free by deleting and reinserting on a hit. A TTL needs a timestamp per entry, which means storing an object rather than the raw value.

In dynamic programming, memoisation and tabulation are the two forms of the same idea. Top-down memoisation starts from the full problem and recurses into subproblems, caching each; bottom-up tabulation starts from the base cases and fills a table forward until the answer is reached. Top-down is easier to derive because it mirrors the recurrence, and it only computes the subproblems that are actually reachable. Bottom-up avoids recursion depth entirely and has better locality, and it is easier to optimise the space down to a few rows when each state depends only on the previous ones.

Recognising a dynamic programming problem is about structure: overlapping subproblems, where the same smaller question is asked repeatedly, and optimal substructure, where the answer to a larger question is built from optimal answers to smaller ones. The recurrence is the specification and the code should follow it literally in the top-down version. Knapsack, edit distance, longest common subsequence, coin change and shortest paths in a DAG are the canonical shapes, and each has a one-dimensional table plus two nested loops as its bottom-up form.

Space optimisation is where the bottom-up form shines. If each row of the table depends only on the previous row, two rows suffice; if each cell depends only on the previous and the current cell, one row suffices, provided the update order within the row is correct for the direction of dependency. Getting that direction wrong produces an answer that is plausible and wrong, which is worse than a crash. When optimising the space, always keep the full-table version in the test suite and compare the two on random inputs before trusting the compact one.
